rewritten_text:
Tom managed to gouge the cupboard with it and was preparing to attack the bureau when he was called away to get dressed for Sunday school.

Mary gave him a tin basin filled with water and a piece of soap. He carried them outside and set the basin on a small bench by the door. Then he dipped the soap, put it down, rolled up his sleeves, and carefully poured the water onto the ground. Returning to the kitchen, he began energetically drying his face on the towel behind the door. Mary took the towel away.

'Aren't you ashamed, Tom? You mustn't behave like that. Water won't hurt you.'

Tom felt a little embarrassed. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a while, gathering his courage. Then he drew a deep breath and began. When he came back into the kitchen, eyes tightly shut and hands feeling for the towel, water and soapsuds dripped honorably from his face as evidence of his efforts. Yet the result, once he emerged from the towel, remained unsatisfactory. The clean area ended at his chin and jawline, like a mask. Beyond its borders stretched a dark expanse of unwatered soil, extending down his front and around his neck. Mary took charge. By the time she finished, he was a man and a brother without any distinction of color, his soaking hair neatly brushed and its short curls arranged in a pretty, balanced pattern. In private, he painstakingly flattened the curls and plastered his hair against his head; he considered curls unmanly, and his own were a constant source of bitterness. Mary then brought out the suit he had worn only on Sundays for the past two years. It was known simply as his 'other clothes,' which tells us how extensive his wardrobe was. Once he had dressed, she straightened him up, buttoned his tidy short jacket to the chin, folded his enormous shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him clean, and crowned him with his speckled straw hat. He looked enormously improved and thoroughly uncomfortable. His discomfort matched his appearance: being clean and wearing clothes without holes imposed a restraint he found irritating. He hoped Mary would overlook his shoes, but that hope soon died. She rubbed them generously with tallow, as people customarily did, and brought them to him. He lost his temper and complained that he was forever being forced to do everything he didn't want to do.

You will be glad to hear that the undertaking you feared so much has begun without disaster. I arrived here yesterday, and my first duty is to reassure my dear sister that I am well and increasingly confident of success.

I am already far north of London. Walking through the streets of Petersburgh, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks, strengthening me and filling me with delight. Can you understand that feeling? The wind has come from the very regions I am heading toward, giving me a taste of their icy weather. Encouraged by this promising breeze, my daydreams grow more vivid and intense. I try without success to believe that the pole is a place of ice and emptiness. In my imagination, it always appears beautiful and delightful. There, Margaret, the sun never disappears: its broad circle moves along the horizon and fills the world with constant light. There—if you will allow me to trust earlier explorers—snow and frost are absent. A peaceful sea may carry us to a land more wonderful and beautiful than any yet discovered in the inhabited world. Its natural life and landscape may be unlike anything known, just as the movements of heavenly bodies surely are in those unexplored spaces. What might we not find in a country of endless daylight? I may discover the mysterious force that draws the compass needle. I may also explain a thousand observations of the heavens whose apparent irregularities need only this voyage to become clear and consistent forever. I will satisfy my eager curiosity by seeing a part of the world nobody has visited and perhaps walking on land no human foot has ever touched. These hopes attract me strongly enough to overcome every fear of danger or death. They send me on this difficult voyage with the same joy a child feels setting off in a little boat with holiday friends to explore the river where he lives. Even if all my guesses prove false, you cannot deny the enormous benefit I would bring humanity, through all future generations, by discovering a route near the pole to countries that now take months to reach. Or I may discover the secret of magnetism, which, if it can be discovered at all, requires an expedition like mine.

Thinking of these things has calmed the agitation with which I began this letter. My heart now glows with an enthusiasm that seems to lift me to heaven. Nothing brings the mind so much peace as a firm purpose, a single point on which the soul can focus its thoughts.

When the wedding took place about three weeks later, St. Peter's overflowed with fashionable guests. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service with tremendous dignity, and everyone agreed that they had never seen a better-looking bride and groom. But their beauty was only part of it: they were happy. Lord Arthur never regretted for a moment everything he had endured for Sybil. She, in turn, gave him the finest gifts a woman could offer a man: adoration, tenderness, and love. Reality never destroyed their romance. They always felt young.

Several years later, after the birth of their two beautiful children, Lady Windermere visited them at Alton Priory. This lovely old property had been the Duke's wedding gift to his son. One afternoon she sat beneath a lime tree in the garden with Lady Arthur, watching the little boy and girl dart like flickering sunbeams along the rose walk. Suddenly she took her hostess's hand. 'Are you happy, Sybil?'

'Dear Lady Windermere, of course I'm happy. Aren't you?'

'I haven't time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the newest person I'm introduced to. But usually, once I get to know people, they bore me.'

'Don't your celebrated guests satisfy you, Lady Windermere?'

'Goodness, no! Social lions are only worth having for a season. Once their manes are trimmed, they're the dullest creatures imaginable. Besides, if you're truly kind to them, they behave appallingly. Remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was an outrageous fraud. Naturally, that didn't bother me in the least. I even forgave him for asking to borrow money. But I couldn't tolerate his romantic advances. He quite turned me against palmistry. I'm interested in telepathy now; it's much more entertaining.'

'You mustn't criticize palmistry here, Lady Windermere. It's the one subject Arthur doesn't like people making fun of. I assure you, he takes it very seriously.'

'Sybil, surely you're not telling me he believes in it?'

'Ask him yourself, Lady Windermere. Here he comes.' Lord Arthur approached through the garden, a large bunch of yellow roses in his hand and his two children dancing around him.

'Lord Arthur?'

'Yes, Lady Windermere?'

'Surely you don't actually believe in palmistry?'

'Of course I do,' the young man said, smiling.

'But why?'

'Because I owe it all the happiness in my life,' he murmured, dropping into a wicker chair.
